title: Portugal Suspends Cristiano Ronaldo Pending Disciplinary Probe After Camp Walkout
excerpt: The 41-year-old faces one to six months under federation rules for leaving the squad in September; federation president Pedro Proença says the FPF, the coach and his teammates all want him back.
body:
• The Portuguese Football Federation has provisionally suspended Cristiano Ronaldo and opened disciplinary proceedings against him for walking out of the national team camp in late September.
  • Under federation regulations, leaving a national team activity without justification carries a suspension of one to six months plus a fine; Ronaldo has apologized, accepted responsibility and says he expects punishment.
  • The walkout followed a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus over playing time: Ronaldo says he was promised about 30 minutes in the Sept. 27 win over Norway but was never sent on, while Jesus denied making any such promise.
  • FPF president Pedro Proença expects the 41-year-old back during the November international break for the final Nations League group games — Denmark on Nov. 14 and Wales on Nov. 17 — suggesting the final sanction could be short.

The Portuguese Football Federation has suspended Cristiano Ronaldo and initiated disciplinary proceedings against the forward for walking out on the national team during the September international window. The federation announced the decision in a statement on Saturday, Oct. 10, saying the case was referred to its disciplinary investigation committee, with findings to remain confidential until the investigation concludes.

The suspension is provisional while the case is investigated. According to a statement reported by Lisbon-based newspaper A Bola, the FPF's Non-Professional Section opened proceedings on Oct. 9 to determine the disciplinary relevance of the facts reported on Oct. 7, ordered a non-automatic provisional suspension of the player, and classified the proceedings as urgent. Ronaldo had already been subject to an automatic provisional suspension until the proceedings were opened.

The walkout that started it

The confrontation traces back to Sept. 27, when Portugal beat Norway 2-1 in Oslo in the UEFA Nations League. Ronaldo warmed up on the touchline as a substitute but was never sent on. In a statement of nearly 2,000 words released earlier this week, Ronaldo said an assistant coach had told him he would play around 30 minutes — and that Jesus broke his word twice: first by not using him in Oslo, and then by failing to stick to a supposedly pre-approved explanation at a press conference before the Denmark match.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=EOafTdp8AHM

Jesus denied making any such promise. Ronaldo declined to acknowledge the traveling fans after the final whistle in Oslo, walking straight down the tunnel. He then departed the team's Copenhagen base on Sept. 30 — a day before Portugal faced Denmark — telling the federation he was leaving, though it remains unclear whether that will be judged sufficient justification under the regulations.

In his statement, Ronaldo apologized to supporters and teammates for leaving mid-window. He wrote that he knew the rules applied to him like everyone else and that he expected a suspension under federation rules — while adding that fans would get "one or more farewell matches."

"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team."

— Cristiano Ronaldo, in his statement this week

Portugal moves on without its captain

The federation's disciplinary rules state that any player who "abandons or fails to appear" without justification at a national-team training session, match or activity faces a suspension of one to six months, in addition to a fine reported at between €500 and €1,000. At best, Ronaldo's suspension could end by late October, making him eligible for the November break; at worst, a six-month ban would keep him out until March 2026 and the June international window.

On the field, Portugal have not missed him. The team won all four of its Nations League group games — including the three played after the 41-year-old left — booking a quarterfinal place with two matches to spare and sitting top of Group A4. His replacement, Gonçalo Ramos, seized the starting role with three goals, strengthening the case that Jesus's side can function — even flourish — without its iconic captain.

Jesus left the door open in a press conference after the Norway win, saying, "If he wants to, he'll return to the national team."

What it means for the chase

Ronaldo, Portugal's all-time leader with 234 caps and 146 goals, is hunting one of football's landmark numbers: 1,000 career goals. He reached No. 980 on Friday, scoring in his first club appearance since the walkout as Al-Nassr beat Diriyah 3-0, with fans showing visible support for the five-time Ballon d'Or winner. Every international appearance in November's fixtures matters if he wants to keep that chase alive in a Portugal shirt.

In India, where Ronaldo commands one of his largest global fan bases, the saga has dominated sports coverage — a reminder of how closely the diaspora follows the final chapters of a career that has spanned nearly 25 years at the top.

What's next

The urgent classification means the disciplinary committee could reach a conclusion before the November break, when Portugal completes its Nations League group campaign: at home to Denmark on Nov. 14 and away to Wales on Nov. 17. Proença has already signaled the federation's preference, saying he expects Ronaldo back then.

"The Federation, the coach and all of Cristiano's team-mates are aligned: we want Cristiano back."

— Pedro Proença, president of the Portuguese Football Federation

"I expect him back already during the November international break," Proença said, adding that Ronaldo himself is willing to return. Whether the disciplinary committee shares that timetable — or hands down the harshest version of the one-to-six-month range — will decide whether the country's most decorated player ends 2026 in a Portugal shirt or watching from afar.
